newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FOCUS-Israeli cabinet approves budget cut.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Israeli cabinet approves budget cut.

text.p: The Israeli cabinet on Monday approved further budget cuts which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said were needed to put the economy back on track and maintain Israel's financial health.
Government officials said the cabinet voted 14-4 in favour of the 1.2 billion shekel ($366 million) cut in state spending at the end of an eight-hour session.

"If we don't cut, let there be no doubt that we will pay with a deterioration in our standing in the financial markets and in our credit rating," a statement quoted Netanyahu as telling the cabinet before the vote.
The cutback comes on top of the 4.9 billion shekels already slashed from the original 1997 budget of 190.8 billion shekels which parliament must ratify before December 31.
"We are presenting another cut because it became clear to us that revenues have not met our expectations," Meridor told Israel Radio before the cabinet meeting started.
"Today, the world is watching us -- investors, banks and governments -- to see...whether the government will fix what has gone wrong in the economy in the last two years," he said.
Economists said government revenues have fallen below projections and the prospect of increased government borrowing has pushed up interest rates, strengthened the shekel and sucked in imports.
As a result Israel's current account deficit is expected to widen to more than $5 billion this year from $4.1 billion in 1995.
Treasury sources had originally put the additional cutbacks in government spending at 1.8 billion shekels.

But Netanyahu said earlier on Monday that Meridor had found "several sources (of income), which do not involve raising taxes, worth over half a billion shekels", bringing the real cut down to 1.2 billion shekels.

The Treasury sources said the proposals included the already announced sale of government-owned homes in Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank, a move certain to draw Arab and international ire. Some 3,000 homes will be sold.
Israel Radio said the government would also abolish several tax exemptions to raise revenues.
Netanyahu accused the Labour government which he defeated in May elections of managing the economy "terribly" and said his administration would "correct the financial system".
Former prime minister Shimon Peres dismissed the criticism, telling Israel Radio: "They were four wonderful years for the Israeli economy, it grew like yeast".
Legislators have said the reductions, widely reported to target spending on social welfare and education, would hit lower-income Israelis hardest.
The Treasury has yet to spell out publicly exactly what the proposed cuts entail.
The announcement of cabinet approval for the cuts was made after the close of trading on the Tel Aviv stock market.
